prize_parts.citation: For empirical analysis of how trade exposure and technological change reshape local labour markets, employment and wage inequality.

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from B012 (Kiyotaki and Moore) to B038 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn). The change is moderate, and the two candidates are close for me. The reasons are substantive. In round 1, the three main reservations about B012 were overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, mixed direct identification of the collateral channel, and a narrow base resting largely on one seminal paper. Hassler, Friberg and Strömberg each raised some version of these. I still think the mechanism is rigorous and well attributed to the two originators, and nothing in the exchange weakened that. But I now give more weight to those three reservations than I did in my opening, and I am wary that my macro background made me more comfortable with the mechanism than the common criteria justify. On B038, the exchange answered the attribution problem I raised in round 1. The task-framework lineage (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu) can be left out of the citation, and the China-shock and local labour-market evidence is jointly the work of Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Enflo, Fredriksson, Hjalmarsson and Krusell all converged on Dorn rather than Katz, and I agree that this is the coherent trio. The contribution combines new measurement, a transparent design and a durable finding of concentrated, persistent local adjustment costs. It has more than a decade of replication, critique and extension, and it has changed research in labour, trade and public economics. My citation covers only empirical analysis of exposure and adjustment. It does not claim the task framework. I do not rely on the number of members who named B038; I treat that as no evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still that B038 bundles two programmes. A citation limited to trade and technology exposure and local adjustment is defensible, but it leaves the task framework, which is the more conceptual half, outside the prize. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects are debated, and shift-share identification has been criticised. I read that debate as refinement of inference and not as overturning the basic finding, but I cannot rule out that further work will lower the magnitudes. There is thematic proximity to the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity, and to recent labour-market prizes. I think the overlap is in the theme and not in the contribution. A committee that weights overlap heavily could reasonably prefer B012 or B002. B012 has the narrower base and the 2022 proximity. B002 is younger and depends on restricted data.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B012 a very close third and doubts that the 2022 overlap is a non-issue, since credit-constraint amplification sits near the banks-and-crises theme. He sees no quality gap between B012 and B041, only a difference in how much new ground each opens relative to prior prizes.
responses.response: I take this seriously and it is part of why I moved. I still think Kiyotaki-Moore, with its borrower-side collateral and asset-price feedback, differs from the 2022 bank-run and intermediation work. But I cannot show that a committee would see the difference as clearly as I do. I would not call the overlap decisive. Under common criteria, though, I should not rank a candidate first when its distinctiveness from earlier recognition is this arguable and a comparably strong candidate has less of that exposure. I keep B012 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B038 seventh. He doubts that shift-share identification withstands scrutiny and says the task framework owes much to uncredited scholars. He would be more comfortable if the achievement were defined as the China-shock evidence alone.
responses.response: The citation I now propose is in that form: empirical analysis of trade and technology exposure and local adjustment, without claiming the task framework. I agree that the shift-share critique is real. Where I differ is that the finding of large, persistent local adjustment costs does not rest on one instrument. It has been examined with different outcomes, pre-trend checks and alternative designs. I accept that magnitudes remain uncertain, and I would keep the citation away from any claim about their size. You also called direct identification of the collateral channel contested in B012, and I now count that against my earlier first choice.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from Katz to Dorn and anchors B038 in the trade-exposure and local-labour-market evidence. He says he would not claim the whole task framework for the trio, and that the attribution is defensible but not unique.
responses.response: I agree with this framing, and your move to Dorn is what I argued in round 1. Katz's contribution on skill demand and the education-technology race is major, but it is a different citation and a different strand. I also agree that the attribution is defensible and not unique, and I would say so openly. Where I differ from you is on the 2024 overlap. I co-wrote a popular summary of that prize, and it rewarded work on institutions and long-run prosperity. That is a different object from local labour-market adjustment to trade and technology shocks.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B038 first. She argues that the shift-share debate has refined and not overturned the main findings. She also argues that uncertainty about magnitudes should not count against a discovery of this kind, and that a citation limited to what Autor, Dorn and Hanson established is defensible.
responses.response: I agree with the limited citation and with your reading of the identification debate. I would qualify the claim that magnitude uncertainty does not count against it. It counts somewhat, because a prize on a measured effect is exposed if later work shrinks it. I think it counts less here than it would for a prize built on a precise number. The qualitative finding of concentrated, lasting local adjustment costs is what the prize would honour. That is why I put B038 ahead of B012, whose mechanism has less direct empirical support.

responses.point: Teorell withdrew Gertler from B012 and keeps Kiyotaki and Moore as an alternative. He ranks B002 first, ranks B038 only fifth, and would limit any B038 citation to the trade-shock contribution.
responses.response: I agree that the two-person form is the strongest version of B012, and your withdrawal of Gertler supports it. On B038 we agree about the citation. A prize defined around the China-shock contribution is the only form I would support. We differ on B002 versus B038 mainly on maturity and on how well the findings can be checked independently. B038 has had longer independent replication and critique. B002 depends on restricted administrative data and its long-run causal results are still developing.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B002 first. She stresses transparent measurement, large samples and credible quasi-experimental design, and she treats the restricted-data constraint as a real discount on maturity that should not be a footnote.
responses.response: I think the measurement and design quality of B002 is exceptional, and I agree the data-access constraint is a real discount. This is the answer to the chair's question on what would raise my confidence: long-run follow-up of the causal place-effect estimates, and agreement from comparable register-based studies in other countries. That evidence is still accumulating. For this reason I keep B002 as an alternative and not as my lead. If the committee prefers it, I support the three-name version with Friedman over the Chetty-Hendren pair. I agree with you that Friedman's role fits the measurement and data-infrastructure description of the discovery better than Katz does.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a B038 citation limited to trade and technology exposure and local adjustment, and whether that leaves the more conceptual task framework outside the prize in a way that makes the prize look narrow.
How far the size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the shift-share identification debate, should lower confidence in the core finding.

Whether the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises leaves enough distinct ground for Kiyotaki-Moore. I am less sure than in round 1, and the same uncertainty applies to my reading of the 2024 overlap for B038.
Whether my move from B012 reflects a real reweighting of the common criteria or an overcorrection after hearing colleagues. The gap between the two is small, and I hold it with limited confidence.
Whether B002 will have enough long-run robustness evidence and independent register-based replication to be judged mature, and whether the third name should be Friedman.
My assessments rely on the supplied evidence and general knowledge without independent source verification.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Autor, Dorn or Hanson is apparent from the supplied profile, and Katz is not in my configuration. The previous first choice, B012, also had no apparent connection. I am a macroeconomist, so I may be more familiar with the macro-finance literature than with the labour-market evidence, and I read that familiarity as a possible source of bias toward B012 in round 1. I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and a co-author of John Hassler (chair), and an IIES colleague of both. Neither is credited on B038, B012 or B002. Peter Klenow, a long-time co-author, is credited on B023, which is not in my configuration or alternatives. I also collaborate long-term with Aghion, Bergeaud, Klenow and Li on creative destruction. That is adjacent in theme to the 2025 prize but does not touch any candidate on my shortlist. My CV lists co-authorship of the Ekonomisk Debatt summaries of the 2024 and 2025 prizes. That informs how I read the overlap between B038 and recent prizes, and it is not a candidate connection. The 2025 Scientific Background cites my work, and a stamp on it may suggest I helped draft it, which is weak evidence. It does not bear on this year's candidates. I have not adjudicated any of these ties.
